blocks.userQuestion: I have been noted in default — can I still fight this?
blocks.whatsHappening: You have been noted in default. This means the clerk has recorded that you did not file a defence in time. No judgment has been signed yet.
blocks.whatToDoNext: You may bring a motion to set aside the noting in default. To succeed, you must show that you have a meritorious defence and a reasonable explanation for the default. The motion must be made as soon as is reasonably possible in all the circumstances.
blocks.whatHappensAfter: If the court is satisfied with your motion, it may set aside the noting in default or any default judgment against you.

citations.quote: The court may set aside the noting in default or default judgment against a party and any step that has been taken to enforce the judgment, on such terms as are just, if the party makes a motion to set aside and the court is satisfied that, (a) the party has a meritorious defence and a reasonable explanation for the default; and (b) the motion is made as soon as is reasonably possible in all the circumstances.

If a defendant to a plaintiff's claim or a defendant's claim fails to file a defence to all or part of the claim with the clerk within the prescribed time, the clerk may note the defendant in default on the filing of, (a) a request to note the defendant in default, which may be made in Form 9B; and (b) proof that the claim was served within the court's territorial division, subject to subrule (3).

blocks.userQuestion: I have been sued — what do I have to do, and by when?
blocks.whatsHappening: You have been served with a claim. You need to respond by delivering a Defence (Form 9A) within 20 days of being served.
blocks.whatToDoNext: Complete the Defence (Form 9A). Serve a copy on every other party. File the Defence with proof of service at the court office indicated on the claim.
blocks.yourDeadline: Serve a defence on every other party and file it with the clerk, with proof of service. You have 20 days, counted from the day of being served with the claim.
blocks.whatHappensAfter: If you do not file your Defence within the 20 days, the plaintiff can request to note you in default. This may lead to a judgment against you without further notice.

citations.quote: A defendant who wishes to dispute a plaintiff's claim shall, within 20 days of being served with the claim, (a) serve on every other party a defence (Form 9A); and (b) file the defence, with proof of service, with the clerk.

If these rules or an order of the court prescribe a period of time for the taking of a step in a proceeding, the time shall be counted by excluding the first day and including the last day of the period; if the last day of the period of time falls on a holiday, the period ends on the next day that is not a holiday.

If a defendant to a plaintiff's claim or a defendant's claim fails to file a defence to all or part of the claim with the clerk within the prescribed time, the clerk may note the defendant in default on the filing of, (a) a request to note the defendant in default, which may be made in Form 9B; and (b) proof that the claim was served within the court's territorial division, subject to subrule (3).
A settlement conference shall be held in every defended action.

blocks.userQuestion: It has been more than six months and I never served them — is my case dead?
blocks.whatsHappening: The claim was issued more than six months ago and has still not been served. You have not served the claim within the required six-month period.
blocks.whatToDoNext: You may file a motion to request an order to extend the time for service. In your motion, you must explain to the judge why you were not able to serve the claim within the six months.
blocks.whatHappensAfter: The court may extend the time for service, before or after the six months has elapsed.

citations.quote: A claim shall be served within six months after the date it is issued, but the court may extend the time for service, before or after the six months has elapsed.
The court may lengthen or shorten any time prescribed by these rules or an order, on such terms as are just.
